claims.text: The initial material is cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr has poor or rapid oxidation in high-temperature air.
Pack aluminization will deposit a thin aluminide layer on HfNbTaTiZr.
The resulting aluminide coating will be uniform and adherent.
During high-temperature exposure in air, the aluminide coating will convert into a continuous Al2O3 scale.
The resulting Al2O3 scale will be dense and slow-growing.
A continuous alumina scale will slow oxygen ingress into the alloy.
Pack aluminization will leave the bulk microstructure of HfNbTaTiZr unaltered.
Aluminized specimens will have lower oxidation-induced mass gain than untreated specimens after exposure in air at 1000 °C.
Aluminized specimens will have thinner oxide scales than untreated specimens after exposure in air at 1000 °C.
Aluminized specimens will retain the room-temperature tensile ductility of untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr.
Aluminized specimens will retain the high-temperature yield strength of untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed oxidation boundary is air at approximately 1000 °C for 50–100 hours.
Mechanical testing should use the same strain-rate and temperature conditions as the baseline tests.
A failure to reduce both mass gain and oxide thickness by at least 50% relative to untreated controls would falsify the oxidation-resistance hypothesis.
A statistically significant degradation in room-temperature ductility or high-temperature yield strength would falsify the mechanical-retention hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions call for tensile and creep testing under the baseline high-temperature conditions, but the experiment specifies room-temperature tensile testing and high-temperature creep testing while also listing yield strength at 1000 °C as a measurement. As written, no high-temperature tensile test is specified to obtain that yield strength.
